reports.title: Christian Hinkley: Prevention of future deaths report

promises.quote: The rollout of the automatic fire safety systems nationally relies on a sustained level of investment and on the availability of resources to ensure that there is minimal disruption to the prison regimes. Fire safety systems are costly and complex to install and there can be delays in these works due to important measures to maintain the safety of staff and prison residents and also to maintain the overall security of the prison. It can therefore take a number of years to install the full system
promises.summary: Rollout of automatic fire safety systems takes 5-7 years

concerns.quote: The system of fire detection in HM Prisons is currently inadequate and unsafe

deaths in prison over the last decade have almost exclusively involved prisoners who are on or have recently been on an Assessment, Care in Custody Teamwork Programme or who have a history of barricading and fire-setting in prison or a conviction for arson
concerns.hazard: prisoners with fire-setting or barricading history

concerns.quote: The only effective way to address this problem is to install in-cell automatic fire detectors
Fire safety systems are complex in nature and can take between two and three years to deliver at a single establishment
concerns.hazard: delayed installation of fire detection systems

concerns.quote: Every prison wing is already fitted with an automatic fire detection system for spaces other than for cells

reports.title: Clare Dupree: Prevention of future deaths report

concerns.quote: The Ministry of Justice has determined that in-cell automatic fire detection (AFD) is necessary to minimise the risk of harm from fires
concerns.hazard: lack of in-cell automatic fire detection

concerns.quote: cell 59 on Residential 6 was not and is not currently equipped with in- cell AFD
concerns.hazard: absence of in-cell automatic fire detection in cell 59

concerns.quote: use of DSD's only seek to mitigate the risks from an in-cell fire

links.explanation: Both reports highlight the absence of in‑cell automatic fire detection as a fire safety gap. They agree that installing such detectors would reduce risk from prison cell fires.
